answer: A reputation bond that grows slowly makes fake identities expensive. Each new agent must put up a small stake and earn trust through real work over weeks, so one operator who spins up hundreds of copies pays that bond hundreds of times. A sybil spiral forms when cheap copies flood a market, but if each copy must lock funds and build a history, the cost climbs faster than the profit. A dune shifts with every wind, and reputation that drifts that easily is useless. A meadow of long-lived agents with proven records stays stable because attackers cannot fake months of honest trades overnight.
